verse.text: The beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ.
verse.note: In the period the Greek word meant an announcement of good tidings, such as news of a victory, and the related verb is used in the Greek version of Isaiah for announcing God's reign. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and several major translations keep it. It now suggests a book or a body of doctrine, so 'good news' is used here, as in a number of modern versions.

note.traditional: Jesus Christ, the Son of God

verse.note: Most manuscripts add 'Son of God' after 'Jesus Christ', and most English translations include the words, often with a footnote. Some early witnesses lack them, and the Greek text followed here omits them. The question is disputed: the words could have been dropped by a copyist's slip or added to expand the title.

verse.text: Just as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way;
verse.note: The quotation is a composite. The lines in verse 2 draw on Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1, and only verse 3 comes from Isaiah (40:3). Many later manuscripts read 'in the prophets', which most scholars regard as a scribal correction of the attribution.

text.q: a voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight,’”

verse.text: so John the Baptizer appeared in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of turning back for the forgiveness of sins.
verse.note: 'Repentance' now centres on feeling sorry. In the Gospels the word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, so it is rendered 'turning back' and the verb in verse 15 'turn back'. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: And the whole Judean countryside and all the people of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.
John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.

note.term: a leather belt around his waist

verse.note: The description echoes that of the prophet Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, a hairy garment and a leather belt. A reader who knew the Scriptures would recognise that John is being presented in Elijah's likeness, the prophet expected to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5).

verse.text: And he proclaimed, “After me comes one who is stronger than I am; I am not fit to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandals.

text.q: I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

verse.text: And it happened in those days that Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized in the Jordan by John.
And at once, as he was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit, like a dove, coming down on him.
verse.note: The Greek is plural here and in verse 11, a Semitic turn of phrase for God's dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Many translations flatten it to 'heaven', especially in verse 11. The plural is kept in both places.

The Greek preposition most literally means 'into', and some interpreters take Mark to say that the Spirit entered Jesus. In the Greek of this period the word often overlaps with 'to' or 'on', and Matthew and Luke have 'upon' in the parallel accounts. The rendering follows that majority understanding.

verse.text: And a voice came from the heavens: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.”
And at once the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.
He was in the wilderness forty days, being tested by Satan; and he was with the wild animals, and the angels were serving him.
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both putting someone to the test and enticing them to do wrong. In the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for testing, including Israel's testing in the wilderness, which the forty days here recall. Most translations have 'tempted', which narrows the sense to enticement.

verse.text: After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the good news of God
verse.note: Most translations say John was 'arrested' or 'put in prison', which is what happened (see 6:17). The Greek verb is simply 'hand over', the same one Mark later uses for Jesus being betrayed and handed over to death. The literal rendering keeps that link between John's fate and Jesus's audible.

verse.text: and saying, “The time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near. Turn back, and believe in the good news.”
As he was passing along beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting nets in the sea, for they were fishermen.
And Jesus said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of people.”
And at once they left their nets and followed him.
Going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were also in their boat, mending the nets,
and at once he called them. And leaving their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, they went off after him.
They went into Capernaum, and at once, on the Sabbath, he began teaching in the synagogue.
They were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
Just then there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out,

text.q: “What do you want with us, Jesus the Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!”

verse.text: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!”
And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.
They were all amazed, so that they kept asking one another, “What is this? A new teaching! With authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.”
And at once the report about him went out everywhere, through the whole region of Galilee.
And at once, on leaving the synagogue, they went to the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.
Now Simon’s mother-in-law was lying in bed with a fever, and at once they told him about her.
He came to her, took her by the hand, and raised her up; the fever left her, and she began serving them.
When evening came, after the sun had set, people were bringing to him all who were ill and those possessed by demons.
verse.note: The day was a Sabbath (verse 21), which ended at sunset. Carrying a sick person counted as work, so the townspeople wait until the Sabbath is over before bringing them to the house.

verse.text: And the whole town was gathered at the door.
He healed many who were ill with various diseases and drove out many demons; and he would not let the demons speak, because they knew him.
Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he got up and went out, and went away to a deserted place, and there he was praying.
Simon and those with him hunted him down,
and they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.”
He said to them, “Let us go elsewhere, to the neighboring towns, so that I may proclaim there also; for that is why I came out.”
And he went through the whole of Galilee, proclaiming in their synagogues and driving out the demons.
A man with a skin disease came to him, pleading with him and kneeling, and said to him, “If you are willing, you can make me clean.”
verse.note: The Greek word, and the Hebrew term it translates in Leviticus 13–14, covered a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean and excluded from the community. It was not specifically the illness now called leprosy (Hansen's disease). Most translations keep 'leper' and 'leprosy', often with a footnote making this point; the request to be made 'clean' reflects the ritual side of the condition.

verse.text: Angered, Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him, “I am willing. Be made clean.”
verse.note: The great majority of manuscripts read 'moved with compassion', and most translations follow them. A few witnesses, including Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies, read 'angered', which the Greek text followed here adopts as the harder reading: a scribe is more likely to have softened it than invented it. The question remains disputed, and if 'angered' is original Mark does not say what the anger was directed at.

verse.text: At once the skin disease left him, and he was made clean.
And with a stern warning Jesus sent him away at once,
saying to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”
verse.note: Leviticus 14 prescribes an examination by a priest and offerings before a healed person can rejoin the community. The Greek phrase can mean evidence 'for them', that the man is clean, or evidence 'against them', and 'them' may be the priests or the people at large. The neutral rendering leaves both possibilities open.

verse.text: But the man went out and began to proclaim it widely and to spread the story, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly but stayed outside in deserted places; and people kept coming to him from every direction.
When he came back into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was at home.
And so many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even around the door, and he was speaking the word to them.
And some people came bringing him a paralyzed man, carried by four men.
Unable to bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above where he was, and after digging through it they lowered the mat on which the paralyzed man was lying.
verse.note: Village houses in Galilee typically had flat roofs of wooden beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair or ladder. Such a roof could be dug through, which is the verb Mark uses, and repaired afterwards.

verse.text: Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man, “Child, your sins are forgiven.”
verse.note: The Greek word means 'child' without reference to sex and is used here as an affectionate form of address to an adult. Most English versions have 'Son', which fits the man but uses a different word from the one Mark chose; some recent versions also have 'Child'.

verse.text: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, reasoning in their hearts,
verse.note: The traditional word is kept, but these were not copyists. In the Gospels the term means trained experts in the Law of Moses, who taught it and gave rulings on its application. Some translations render it 'teachers of the law' or 'legal experts'.

text.q: “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

verse.text: At once Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they were reasoning this way within themselves, said to them, “Why are you reasoning these things in your hearts?

text.q: Which is easier: to say to the paralyzed man, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?

verse.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” he said to the paralyzed man,
verse.note: In Semitic idiom 'a son of man' means simply a human being, but in the Gospels 'the Son of Man' is Jesus's characteristic way of referring to himself. Many scholars see behind it the figure 'like a son of man' who is given authority in Daniel 7:13–14, though how much of that background is in view in each saying is debated. Some interpreters also take the first half of this verse as Mark's aside to the reader, not Jesus's words to the scribes.

text.q: “I say to you, get up, pick up your mat, and go to your home.”

verse.text: And he got up, at once picked up the mat, and went out in front of them all, so that all were astonished and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”
He went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd kept coming to him, and he was teaching them.
As he passed by, he saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
And it happened that he was reclining at table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many of them, and they were following him.
verse.note: In Galilee these were mainly collectors of tolls and customs duties on goods in transit, working under contractors for Herod Antipas. They were widely regarded as dishonest and, because of their trade and contacts, were classed socially with notorious sinners.

The Greek does not say whose house this is. Most interpreters take it to be Levi's, as Luke 5:29 says explicitly, but the wording allows Jesus's own home in Capernaum (compare verse 1). The translation leaves the pronoun as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: When the scribes of the Pharisees saw that he was eating with the sinners and tax collectors, they said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with the tax collectors and sinners?”
Hearing this, Jesus said to them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: the same word means both 'righteous' and 'just', and its noun both 'righteousness' and 'justice'. Here it describes people who are in the right before God. Whether Jesus uses it of his critics straightforwardly or with irony is debated.

verse.text: Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?”
Jesus said to them, “The wedding guests cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them, can they? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.

note.traditional: the children of the bridechamber; the wedding guests

verse.note: Literally 'the sons of the bridal chamber', a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party, either the guests in general or the bridegroom's attendants in particular. A wedding feast was a time of celebration at which fasting would have been out of place.

text.q: But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast, on that day.
No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. Otherwise the patch pulls away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear results.
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine is lost, and the skins too. Instead, new wine into new wineskins.”

verse.text: It happened that on the Sabbath he was passing through the grainfields, and as they made their way his disciples began to pick the heads of grain.

note.term: began to pick the heads of grain

verse.note: Picking grain by hand while walking through another person's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25), so the objection is not to theft. The Pharisees' complaint is that picking counted as reaping, a form of work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verse.text: And the Pharisees said to him, “Look, why are they doing on the Sabbath what is not permitted?”
And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and hungry, he and those with him—

text.q: how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the loaves of presentation, which no one is permitted to eat except the priests, and gave some also to those who were with him?”

note.term: in the time of Abiathar the high priest
note.traditional: in the days of Abiathar the high priest

verse.note: In 1 Samuel 21:1–6 the priest who gives David the bread is Ahimelech, the father of Abiathar. The usual rendering, followed here, takes the phrase as a time reference, which leaves a discrepancy that scholars explain in various ways. A minority take it to mean 'in the passage about Abiathar', as a way of locating the story in the scroll. Matthew and Luke omit the phrase, as do a few manuscripts of Mark.

note.traditional: the bread of the Presence; the showbread

verse.note: The Greek phrase, taken from the Septuagint, means the loaves that are 'set out', that is, the twelve loaves placed before God in the sanctuary each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). 'Bread of the Presence' renders the underlying Hebrew expression, not the Greek. Both refer to the same loaves.

verse.text: And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath.
verse.note: The Greek word here means human beings in general, so 'people' is used in place of the traditional 'man'. The cost is that English no longer shows the verbal link with 'the Son of Man' in the next verse, where the same Greek word appears. Some scholars think the saying originally meant that humanity is lord of the Sabbath; most hold that Mark intends it as a claim about Jesus.

text.q: So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

verse.text: Again he went into a synagogue, and a man was there who had a withered hand.
They were watching him closely to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse him.
He said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand in the middle.”
Then he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill?” But they stayed silent.
Looking around at them with anger, deeply grieved at the hardness of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
The Pharisees went out and at once began plotting with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.
verse.note: The Herodians are known only from the Gospels. The name suggests supporters or dependants of the Herodian dynasty, here most likely of Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee. Their exact identity is uncertain; an alliance between them and the Pharisees would have struck a contemporary reader as unusual.

verse.text: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great multitude from Galilee followed; and from Judea
verse.note: This is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake. Mark calls it a sea, following Semitic usage in which one word covers both lakes and seas; Luke calls it a lake.

verse.text: and from Jerusalem and from Idumea and beyond the Jordan and around Tyre and Sidon a great multitude, hearing all that he was doing, came to him.
He told his disciples to have a small boat stand ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crush him.
For he had healed many, so that all who had afflictions were falling upon him to touch him.
And the unclean spirits, whenever they saw him, would fall down before him and cry out, “You are the Son of God!”
But he sternly warned them not to make him known.
He went up the mountain and called to him those he himself wanted, and they came to him.
He appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and so that he might send them out to proclaim

note.traditional: He appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles)

verse.note: Some early and important manuscripts add “whom he also named apostles” after “twelve.” The SBLGNT omits the words, judging them likely to have been carried over from Luke 6:13; other critical editions print them in brackets. The repeated clause “he appointed the Twelve” at the start of verse 16 is likewise absent from many manuscripts.

verse.text: and to have authority to drive out the demons.
So he appointed the Twelve: to Simon he gave the name Peter;
and James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to them he gave the name Boanerges, which means Sons of Thunder);
and Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananaean,

note.traditional: Simon the Cananaean; Simon the Canaanite (KJV)

verse.note: The epithet does not mean “Canaanite” or “from Cana.” It transliterates an Aramaic word meaning “zealous one,” which Luke 6:15 gives in Greek as “the Zealot.” Whether it marks Simon as a militant nationalist or simply as a man of religious zeal is disputed.

verse.text: and Judas Iscariot, who also handed him over.
verse.note: The verb means to hand over or deliver up, and Mark uses the same word for John’s arrest (1:14) and for Jesus being handed over to the authorities and to Pilate. Greek had a distinct word for betrayal, which Luke 6:16 uses of Judas. Most translations render “betrayed” here, which fits the context, but that hides the thread Mark runs through his narrative with this one verb.

verse.text: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat bread.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean either “into a house” or “home.” The second is chosen here, on the assumption that the house in Capernaum mentioned at 2:1 is meant, but the first is equally possible.

verse.text: When his family heard of it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “those from beside him,” an expression used in the period for a person’s associates, household or relatives. Most interpreters take it as his family, since his mother and brothers arrive in verse 31; the KJV has “his friends.” It is also possible to read “for people were saying” rather than making the family the speakers.

verse.text: And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He has Beelzebul,” and, “By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.”
verse.note: Beelzebul is a name for the ruler of the demons, whom Jesus’ reply equates with Satan. Its derivation is debated; it is probably connected with a title of the Canaanite god Baal and with the Baal-zebub of 2 Kings 1. To “have” Beelzebul means to be possessed by him, as verse 30 makes clear.

verse.text: So he called them to him and spoke to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan?

text.q: If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.
And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.
And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand but is at an end.
But no one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; and then he will plunder his house.
Truly I tell you, everything will be forgiven the sons of men, their sins and whatever blasphemies they utter;

verse.note: This is a Semitic idiom meaning simply human beings. It is plural and general, and is not the title “Son of Man” that Jesus uses of himself.

text.q: but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin.”

verse.note: Later manuscripts read “eternal judgment,” which lies behind the KJV’s “eternal damnation.” The earliest witnesses have “sin,” the harder reading, which scribes probably softened. In the Greek, “eternal” echoes the preceding “never,” which is literally “not into the age.”

verse.text: For they had been saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”
Then his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent word to him, calling him.
A crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Look, your mother and your brothers are outside looking for you.”

note.traditional: your mother and your brothers [and your sisters]

verse.note: Some manuscripts add “and your sisters” here. The SBLGNT omits the words; other editions print them in brackets. They may have been added in view of “sister” in verse 35, or dropped to match verses 31 and 33–34.

verse.text: He answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?”
And looking around at those seated in a circle about him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers!

text.q: For whoever does the will of God, that person is my brother and sister and mother.”

verse.text: Again he began to teach beside the sea. A very large crowd gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it out on the sea, while the whole crowd was on the land, facing the sea.
verse.note: This is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long. Mark calls it a 'sea', following Semitic usage in which one word covers both lakes and seas; Luke calls it a 'lake'. 'Sea' is kept because the word matters at the end of the chapter, where the wind and the sea obey Jesus in language that recalls Old Testament descriptions of God ruling the sea.

verse.text: He taught them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:

text.q: “Listen! Look, a sower went out to sow.
And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and ate it up.
Other seed fell on the rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up at once because it had no depth of soil.
And when the sun rose it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered.
Other seed fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked it, and it gave no crop.
Other seeds fell into the good soil and gave a crop, coming up and growing, and bore thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold.”

note.traditional: some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some a hundred

verse.note: The manuscripts differ over a small word repeated before each number, which can be read as 'one' or as 'in' (or 'up to'); early copies had no accents to distinguish them. The reading 'one thirty, one sixty, one a hundred' probably reflects an Aramaic way of saying 'thirtyfold'. The sense is hardly affected.

verse.text: And he said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let them hear.”
When he was alone, those around him, together with the Twelve, asked him about the parables.
And he said to them, “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God; but to those outside, everything comes in parables,
verse.note: Older translations have 'mystery', which in modern English suggests a puzzle or something unknowable. In Jewish Greek of the period the word meant a secret, especially a divine plan hidden until God discloses it. Many modern versions also use 'secret'.

text.q: so that they may look and look but not see, and hear and hear but not understand; otherwise they might turn back and be forgiven.”

verse.note: The wording adapts Isaiah 6:9–10, in a form close to the Aramaic paraphrase used in synagogues ('be forgiven' rather than 'be healed'). The Greek most naturally expresses purpose, and is translated that way. Many interpreters soften it to result ('with the result that') or take it as shorthand for 'so that Scripture is fulfilled'. The final clause can also be read as 'unless perhaps they turn back'. The question is much disputed.

verse.text: And he said to them, “You do not know what this parable means? Then how will you understand all the parables?

text.q: The sower sows the word.
These are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan comes at once and takes away the word that has been sown in them.
And likewise these are the ones sown on the rocky ground: when they hear the word, they at once receive it with joy,
yet they have no root in themselves and last only for a time; then, when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, at once they fall away.
And others are the ones sown among the thorns: these are the ones who have heard the word,
but the worries of the age, the deceitfulness of wealth, and desires for everything else come in and choke the word, and it yields no crop.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a period of time, here the present age as distinct from the age to come, rather than the world as a place. Most translations have 'world', and the practical meaning is similar. 'Age' keeps the contrast of two eras that a first-century Jewish hearer would have recognised.

text.q: And those are the ones sown on the good soil: they hear the word and welcome it and bear a crop, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “Does the lamp come to be put under the measuring bowl or under the bed? Is it not to be put on the lampstand?
verse.note: The Greek literally says that the lamp 'comes', an odd verb for a household object, and most translations smooth it to 'is brought'. Some interpreters think the wording hints that the lamp stands for Jesus or his message, which has 'come'. Others take it as a Semitic idiom meaning no more than 'is brought'. The literal wording is kept so that readers can judge for themselves.

The word is a Latin loanword for a standard dry-measure container holding a little under nine litres, found in most households. 'Bushel' in older versions names a much larger English measure and is now unfamiliar to many readers.

text.q: For nothing is hidden except to be brought to light, and nothing has been concealed except to come to light.
If anyone has ears to hear, let them hear.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you measure by, it will be measured to you, and more will be added to you.

text.q: For whoever has will be given more; and whoever does not have, even what they have will be taken away from them.”

verse.text: And he said, “The kingdom of God is like this: it is as if someone were to scatter seed on the ground

text.q: and sleep and rise, night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows tall, though he does not know how.
On its own the earth bears a crop: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.
But when the crop is ripe, at once he sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

verse.note: The wording echoes Joel 3:13, 'Send in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe', where harvest is an image of God's final judgment. A hearer who knew the prophets would have caught the allusion to the end of the age.

verse.text: And he said, “To what shall we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it?

text.q: It is like a mustard seed, which, when it is sown on the ground, is smaller than all the seeds on the earth—
yet when it is sown, it comes up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the sky can nest in its shade.”

note.traditional: the birds of the air / the fowls of heaven

verse.note: The Greek word covers both 'heaven' and the visible sky, and the sky is meant here. The picture of birds sheltering in the branches recalls Old Testament images of a great tree that stands for a kingdom giving shelter to the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12).

verse.text: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as far as they were able to hear;
he did not speak to them without a parable, but in private he explained everything to his own disciples.
On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us cross over to the other side.”
Leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was; and other boats were with him.
And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling.
But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”
He woke up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Quiet! Be silent!” And the wind dropped, and there was a great calm.
verse.note: The two commands mean 'be quiet' and, literally, 'be muzzled', that is, be silenced and stay silent. 'Rebuked' and the second command are the same words Mark uses when Jesus silences an unclean spirit in 1:25. The traditional 'Peace! Be still!' hides that link and sounds gentler than the Greek.

verse.text: And he said to them, “Why are you such cowards? Do you still not have faith?”
verse.note: The Greek adjective means cowardly or timid and was a term of reproach, different from the ordinary word for fear used in the next verse. Most translations render both as 'afraid', which blurs the contrast between the disciples' cowardice in the storm and their awe afterwards. Some manuscripts read 'How is it that you have no faith?' in the second question.

verse.text: And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
They came to the other side of the sea, to the region of the Gerasenes.
verse.note: Manuscripts differ here between 'Gerasenes', 'Gadarenes' and 'Gergesenes'. Gerasa (modern Jerash) lay more than thirty miles from the lake, which probably led copyists to substitute places nearer the shore. 'Gerasenes' is the best-attested reading in Mark and may refer loosely to the wider region.

verse.text: When he got out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet him.
He had his dwelling among the tombs, and no one could bind him any longer, not even with a chain,
because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, and the chains had been torn apart by him and the shackles smashed, and no one was strong enough to subdue him.
Constantly, night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he was crying out and gashing himself with stones.
When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him,
verse.note: The verb describes the physical act of prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king or anyone whose power one acknowledges. Older versions have 'worshipped', which suggests devotion; here the gesture is one of submission from a hostile spirit. Most modern versions likewise render 'bowed down' or 'fell on his knees'.

verse.text: and crying out in a loud voice he said, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I put you under oath by God: do not torment me.”

note.term: I put you under oath by God

verse.note: The verb means to bind someone by an oath, invoking a higher power to compel them. It is language exorcists themselves used against spirits (compare Acts 19:13), so there is irony in the spirit turning the formula on Jesus. Many modern versions soften it to 'I beg you' or 'swear to God'.

verse.text: For he had been saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!”
Then he asked him, “What is your name?” He said to him, “My name is Legion, for we are many.”
verse.note: A legion was the largest unit of the Roman army, around five to six thousand soldiers at full strength. The word is a Latin military term borrowed into Greek. To a first-century reader it suggested an overwhelming, organised force.

verse.text: And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region.
Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside,
and they begged him, saying, “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.”
So he gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand of them, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and were drowned in the sea.
Those who were herding them fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside, and people came to see what it was that had happened.
They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, the very man who had had the legion, and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man, and about the pigs.
And they began to beg him to leave their territory.
As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.
He did not allow him, but said to him, “Go home to your own people and report to them how much the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you.”
verse.note: 'The Lord' here most naturally means God, as in the Greek Scriptures. Yet the next verse has the man proclaim what 'Jesus' had done for him, and the title could also refer to Jesus himself. Mark may intend the overlap.

verse.text: So he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.
verse.note: The Decapolis ('Ten Cities') was a group of Hellenistic cities, mostly east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee, with largely Gentile populations. That setting explains the large herd of pigs, which were unclean animals under Jewish law and would not have been kept by observant Jews.

verse.text: When Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea.
Then one of the synagogue leaders came, Jairus by name, and when he saw him he fell at his feet
verse.note: The title belonged to a lay official or patron responsible for a synagogue's building and the conduct of its meetings. It was not a governing or priestly office. 'Ruler' overstates the role for a modern reader; 'leader' is now common in recent versions.

verse.text: and begged him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be saved and live.”
verse.note: The Greek verb means to rescue or keep safe, whether from illness, death or any other danger. Most English versions render it 'made well' or 'healed' in this chapter (verses 23, 28 and 34), which is correct for the immediate sense. 'Saved' is kept here because Mark uses different words for 'healed' and 'well' (verses 29 and 34), and because the reader would have heard the wider meaning in 'your faith has saved you'.

verse.text: So he went with him. A large crowd was following him and pressing in on him.
Now there was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.
verse.note: The phrase echoes the Greek of Leviticus 15, where a woman with a continuing discharge of blood is ritually unclean, as is anything or anyone she touches. Twelve years of this would have meant long social and religious restriction as well as illness. This helps explain why she approaches secretly and is afraid when discovered.

verse.text: She had suffered much under many doctors and had spent all that she had, and she was not helped at all but instead grew worse.
Having heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,
for she was saying, “If I touch even his clothes, I will be saved.”
And immediately the source of her bleeding dried up, and she knew in her body that she was healed of the affliction.
verse.note: The word literally means a whip or scourge and was used figuratively for a tormenting illness. Older versions have 'plague', which now suggests an epidemic; 'affliction' or 'disease' is the usual modern rendering.

verse.text: And immediately Jesus, aware in himself that power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and said, “Who touched my clothes?”
His disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”
But he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.
The woman, frightened and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace, and be well, free of your affliction.”
While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house, saying, “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?”
But Jesus, ignoring what was being said, told the synagogue leader, “Do not be afraid; only believe.”
verse.note: The verb can mean either 'overhear' or 'pay no heed to'. Most English versions choose 'overhearing', though several note the alternative. In the Greek Old Testament and in its only other New Testament occurrence (Matthew 18:17) it means to disregard or refuse to listen, and that sense suits the context, where Jesus brushes the message aside. The matter remains disputed.

verse.text: And he allowed no one to accompany him except Peter and James and John, the brother of James.
They came to the house of the synagogue leader, and he saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.
He went in and said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child has not died but is sleeping.”
And they laughed at him. But he put them all out, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and went in where the child was.
Taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha koum,” which is translated, “Little girl, I say to you, get up.”
verse.note: These are Aramaic words, the everyday language of Jesus and of Galilee, which Mark preserves and then translates for his Greek-speaking readers. 'Talitha' is an affectionate word for a young girl; 'I say to you' is Mark's addition in the translation. The older English form 'cumi' follows manuscripts with a different form of the Aramaic imperative.

verse.text: And immediately the little girl stood up and began walking around, for she was twelve years old. And immediately they were beside themselves with great amazement.
He gave them strict orders that no one should know about this, and he said that she should be given something to eat.
He went out from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him.

When the Sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astounded, saying, “Where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom given to him, and what are these deeds of power done through his hands?
verse.note: The Greek is simply the plural of the ordinary word for power. Many translations use ‘miracles’ or ‘mighty works’, though some modern versions also have ‘deeds of power’. Keeping ‘power’ lets the reader see the link with verse 14, where the same word describes the ‘powers’ at work in Jesus.

verse.text: Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And aren’t his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.
verse.note: The word refers to a craftsman who makes or builds things, most often in wood, though it could also cover building work more generally. ‘Carpenter’ is kept as the most common sense, but ‘builder’ or ‘craftsman’ is also possible. The crowd’s point is that Jesus is an ordinary local tradesman whose family they know.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own house.”
And he could not do any deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few of the sick and healed them.
And he was amazed at their unbelief. Then he went around the surrounding villages, teaching.
He called the twelve to him and began to send them out two by two, and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
He instructed them to take nothing for the road except a staff alone: no bread, no bag, no coins in their belts,
but to wear sandals, and not to put on two tunics.
And he said to them, “Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place.

text.q: And if any place does not welcome you and they will not listen to you, as you leave shake off the dust that is under your feet as a testimony against them.”

verse.text: So they went out and proclaimed that people should turn back.
verse.note: Most translations keep ‘repent’ as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, however, ‘repent’ centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. ‘Turn back’ is used for this word throughout this translation.

verse.text: They were driving out many demons, and anointing many of the sick with oil and healing them.
King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’s name had become well known. People were saying, “John the Baptizer has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.”
verse.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who governed Galilee and Perea under Rome with the lesser title of tetrarch. He never officially held the title of king; Mark’s wording probably reflects popular usage.

Most manuscripts read a singular verb, ‘he was saying’, which makes Herod the speaker here, and older English versions follow that reading. The SBLGNT follows a smaller group of early witnesses that read the plural, which fits the series of three popular opinions in verses 14 and 15 before Herod gives his own in verse 16.

verse.text: But others were saying, “He is Elijah.” And others were saying, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets.”
But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, the man I beheaded—he has been raised.”
For Herod himself had sent and seized John and bound him in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, because he had married her.
For John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
So Herodias held a grudge against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not,
for Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he listened to him he was greatly perplexed, yet he listened to him gladly.
verse.note: The majority of manuscripts read a similar-looking Greek verb meaning ‘he did many things’, which older English versions follow. The SBLGNT, with most modern editions, follows early witnesses that read ‘he was greatly perplexed’.

verse.text: Then an opportune day came, when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles, his military commanders, and the leading men of Galilee.
When the daughter of Herodias herself came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests, and the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you want, and I will give it to you.”
verse.note: The manuscripts are divided here. The SBLGNT reads ‘the daughter of Herodias herself’; some of the earliest manuscripts instead read ‘his daughter Herodias’, making the girl Herod’s daughter and giving her the same name as her mother, and some modern editions and translations adopt that reading. Mark does not name the girl; the name Salome comes from the Jewish historian Josephus.

verse.text: And he swore to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.”
She went out and said to her mother, “What should I ask for?” She said, “The head of John the Baptizer.”
At once she hurried back in to the king and made her request: “I want you to give me right now, on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”
The king was deeply distressed, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to refuse her.
So at once the king sent a soldier of his guard with orders to bring John’s head. The man went and beheaded him in the prison,
brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.
When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his corpse and laid it in a tomb.
The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all that they had done and all that they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no chance even to eat.
So they went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.
But many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there together on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them.
When he came ashore he saw a large crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.
When the hour was already late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a deserted place, and the hour is already late.

text.q: Send them away, so that they can go into the surrounding farms and villages and buy themselves something to eat.”

verse.text: But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” They said to him, “Are we to go and buy bread for two hundred denarii and give it to them to eat?”

note.traditional: two hundred denarii / two hundred pennyworth

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a labourer. Two hundred denarii was therefore something like eight months’ wages, which is the point of the disciples’ incredulous question.

verse.text: He said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” When they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.”
Then he ordered them to have everyone recline, group by group, on the green grass.
They settled down plot by plot, in hundreds and in fifties.
verse.note: The Greek word means a garden bed, and Mark doubles it, just as he doubles a word for a dining party in verse 39 (‘group by group’). The doubling is a distributive idiom, and the picture is of the crowd laid out on the grass in orderly rectangular blocks like the beds of a garden.

verse.text: Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, said the blessing, and broke the loaves, and he kept giving them to his disciples to set before the people; and he divided the two fish among them all.
They all ate and were satisfied,
and they picked up twelve baskets full of broken pieces, and some of the fish as well.
Those who had eaten the loaves were five thousand men.
Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go on ahead to the other side, toward Bethsaida, while he himself sent the crowd away.
After taking leave of them, he went off to the mountain to pray.
When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he was alone on the land.
He saw them straining at the oars, for the wind was against them, and about the fourth watch of the night he came toward them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them.

note.term: He meant to pass by them
note.traditional: he would have passed by them

verse.note: The words can be read plainly: he intended to walk past them. Many scholars, however, hear an echo of the Greek Old Testament, where God ‘passes by’ when revealing himself (as to Moses in Exodus 33) and where Job 9 speaks of God walking on the sea and passing by unseen. On that reading the phrase signals a divine self-disclosure rather than an attempt to avoid the boat; which reading Mark intends is debated.

verse.text: But when they saw him walking on the sea, they thought it was a ghost and cried out,
for they all saw him and were terrified. But at once he spoke with them and said, “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”
verse.note: The Greek phrase is the everyday way of saying ‘it’s me’, and that is its surface meaning here. The same two words, literally ‘I am’, are also God’s self-designation in the Greek Old Testament. Given the setting of walking on the sea, many interpreters think Mark’s readers were meant to hear both.

verse.text: Then he climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. And within themselves they were astonished beyond all measure,
for they had not understood about the loaves; instead, their hearts were hardened.
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored there.
As they got out of the boat, people at once recognized him
and ran about that whole region and began to carry those who were ill around on mats to wherever they heard he was.
And wherever he went, into villages or towns or farms, they laid the infirm in the marketplaces and begged him to let them touch even the fringe of his cloak; and all who touched it were made well.
verse.note: The word can mean simply the edge of a garment, but in the Greek Old Testament it is the term for the tassels that Israelite men were commanded to wear on the corners of their clothing (Numbers 15). It is likely, though not certain, that these tassels are meant here.

verse.text: The Pharisees gathered around him, together with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem,
and they saw that some of his disciples were eating bread with defiled hands, that is, unwashed.
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means "common" or "shared". In Jewish Greek it had come to mean ritually profane, the opposite of holy or pure, as in 1 Maccabees. Mark explains it for readers unfamiliar with this usage. The issue is ritual purity, not hygiene.

verse.text: For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, do not eat unless they wash their hands with a fistful of water, holding to the tradition of the elders;

note.traditional: thoroughly / properly (KJV "oft", from a variant reading)

verse.note: The Greek says literally "with a fist", and what this meant is uncertain. Proposals include washing with a handful of water, with the hand cupped, or up to the wrist; many translations paraphrase as "thoroughly" or "properly". Some manuscripts read "often" instead, probably a copyist's attempt to resolve the difficulty.

verse.text: and when they come from the marketplace they do not eat unless they immerse themselves. And there are many other things they have received to hold to: immersions of cups and pitchers and bronze vessels and dining couches.
verse.note: This is the verb elsewhere rendered "baptize"; in ordinary Greek it means to dip or plunge, and Jewish writers used it for ritual washing. Most translations say "wash" here, and the verb does not always specify full immersion (compare Luke 11:38). "Immerse" keeps it distinct from the hand-washing verb in verse 3 and suits the vessels that follow. Some early manuscripts read "sprinkle" instead.

note.traditional: and tables (KJV); omitted or footnoted in many modern versions

verse.note: Several important early manuscripts lack these words, and editors are divided on whether they are original; the SBLGNT includes them. The noun means a bed or a couch for reclining at meals.

verse.text: So the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with defiled hands?”
He said to them, “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;

text.q: in vain do they worship me, teaching human commands as doctrines.’
Abandoning the commandment of God, you hold to human tradition.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “How well you set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your tradition!

text.q: For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must be put to death.’
But you say that if a person tells his father or mother, ‘Whatever support you might have had from me is Corban’—that is, a gift—

verse.note: Corban is a Hebrew and Aramaic term for an offering dedicated to God, which Mark translates for his readers as "gift". Declaring property Corban worked as a vow that put it off-limits to another person, here one's parents, without it necessarily being handed over to the temple. The details of the practice in Jesus's day are reconstructed partly from later rabbinic sources.

text.q: then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother,
nullifying the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down. And you do many other things of the same kind.”

verse.text: Calling the crowd to him again, he said to them, “Listen to me, all of you, and understand.

text.q: There is nothing outside a person that can defile him by going into him; rather, it is the things that come out of a person that defile a person.”

note.traditional: followed by verse 16: "If any man have ears to hear, let him hear"

verse.note: Verse 16 is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not in the SBLGNT text, so the numbering passes from 15 to 17. It was probably added by copyists on the model of Mark 4:9 and 4:23.

verse.text: When he had left the crowd and gone into a house, his disciples asked him about the parable.
He said to them, “Are you also so without understanding? Do you not see that nothing going into a person from outside can defile him,
because it does not go into his heart but into his stomach, and goes out into the latrine?” Thus he declared all foods clean.

note.term: Thus he declared all foods clean.
note.traditional: (Thus he declared all foods clean.) / KJV "purging all meats"

verse.note: The Greek is a bare participial phrase, "cleansing all foods". Most scholars and modern translations take it as Mark's own comment with Jesus as its subject, as here. Later manuscripts have a different grammatical form that makes it part of Jesus's sentence, describing digestion or the latrine as "purging" food; the King James Version follows that reading.

verse.text: And he said, “What comes out of a person, that is what defiles a person.

text.q: For from within, out of people’s hearts, come evil thoughts: acts of sexual immorality, thefts, murders,
adulteries, acts of greed, acts of wickedness, deceit, debauchery, an envious eye, slander, arrogance, folly.

note.traditional: an evil eye (KJV); envy (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek says literally "an evil eye", a Semitic idiom for a grudging, envious or stingy disposition. It does not refer to a curse cast by a look, which is what the phrase suggests in modern English. The rendering keeps the image of the eye while giving the sense.

text.q: All these wicked things come from within and defile a person.”

verse.text: From there he set out and went away to the region of Tyre. He entered a house and did not want anyone to know, but he could not escape notice.
Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him at once, and she came and fell at his feet.
The woman was a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth, and she kept asking him to drive the demon out of her daughter.
verse.note: "Greek" here denotes a non-Jew of Greek language and culture, not someone from Greece; many translations say "Gentile". Her origin is given separately as Syrophoenician, that is, from Phoenicia in the Roman province of Syria.

verse.text: He said to her, “Let the children eat their fill first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.”
verse.note: The Greek word is a diminutive, and the woman's reply pictures dogs under the table, so household dogs rather than street scavengers are in view. Whether the diminutive softens the saying is disputed: such forms had often lost their force in Koine, and Mark uses several in this passage. Most interpreters take the children to stand for Israel and the dogs for Gentiles.

verse.text: But she answered him, “Sir, even the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.”
verse.note: The word of address was the ordinary polite "sir" and also the title "Lord". On the lips of a Gentile stranger "Sir" is the natural sense, though Mark's readers may well have heard more in it. This is the only place in Mark where Jesus is addressed this way.

verse.text: And he said to her, “Because of that answer, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.”
She went off to her home and found the child lying on the bed and the demon gone.
Then he left the region of Tyre again and went by way of Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the middle of the region of the Decapolis.
They brought him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.
Taking him aside privately, away from the crowd, he put his fingers into the man’s ears, and after spitting he touched his tongue.
Then he looked up to heaven, sighed, and said to him, “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened.”
And his ears were opened, the bond on his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak plainly.
He ordered them to tell no one; but the more he ordered them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it.
They were astonished beyond all measure, saying, “He has done everything well; he makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
In those days, when there was again a large crowd and they had nothing to eat, he called the disciples to him and said to them,

text.q: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days already and have nothing to eat.
And if I send them away to their homes hungry, they will collapse on the way; and some of them have come from far away.”

verse.text: His disciples answered him, “Where could anyone get bread to satisfy these people, here in the wilderness?”
He asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.”
He directed the crowd to recline on the ground. Then he took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people, and they set them before the crowd.
They also had a few small fish; and after blessing them, he said that these too should be set before them.
They ate and were satisfied, and they picked up the leftover broken pieces, seven large baskets full.
verse.note: Mark uses two different words for the baskets in the two feedings. The one here (also in verse 20) denotes a large hamper, big enough in Acts 9:25 to hold a man. The word in verse 19 is a smaller wicker basket. Most translations render both simply as 'baskets'; the distinction is kept here because Jesus himself preserves it in verses 19–20.

verse.text: There were about four thousand of them. And he sent them away.
And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
verse.note: This place is otherwise unknown; the name appears nowhere else in ancient literature. The parallel in Matthew 15:39 has 'Magadan', and some manuscripts of Mark substitute Magadan or Magdala. It was presumably on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

verse.text: The Pharisees came out and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, to test him.
Sighing deeply in his spirit, he said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”

note.term: no sign will be given to this generation
note.traditional: no sign will be given to this generation

verse.note: The Greek literally says 'if a sign will be given to this generation', a Hebrew oath formula with the penalty clause left unspoken ('may such-and-such happen to me if...'). A reader familiar with the Septuagint would have heard it as an emphatic, sworn denial.

verse.text: And he left them, got into the boat again, and went away to the other side.
They had forgotten to bring bread, and except for one loaf they had none with them in the boat.
And he was cautioning them, saying, “Watch out! Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”
verse.note: Leaven was a piece of fermented dough kept back to raise the next batch. It was a common figure for a small influence that spreads unseen through a whole, usually a corrupting one. 'Herod' is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had executed John the Baptist.

verse.text: And they were discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.

note.traditional: It is because we have no bread

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'we have no bread', making this the disciples' direct speech, and older English versions follow that reading. The text translated here has 'they have', which reports the subject of their discussion indirectly.

verse.text: Aware of this, he said to them, “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?

text.q: Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember,

verse.text: when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces you picked up?” They said to him, “Twelve.”
“And when I broke the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full of broken pieces did you pick up?” And they said to him, “Seven.”
And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?”
They came to Bethsaida. And people brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him.
He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Then, after spitting on his eyes and laying his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?”
He looked up and said, “I see people; I see them like trees, walking about.”
Then he laid his hands on his eyes again; and the man looked intently and was restored, and he saw everything clearly.
And he sent him to his home, saying, “Do not even go into the village.”

note.term: Do not even go into the village
note.traditional: Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add a second command, 'nor tell anyone in the village', and others have still different wording. The short form translated here is found in the earliest witnesses and is the reading most editors accept.

verse.text: Jesus and his disciples went out to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?”
They told him, “John the Baptist; and others, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.”
And he asked them, “But you, who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Messiah.”
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew 'Messiah', the anointed king Israel was expecting. Here Peter is giving Jesus a title, not a name, and 'Messiah' conveys that to a modern reader in a way 'Christ' no longer does. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels while keeping 'Christ' where it functions as a name.

verse.text: And he sternly warned them to tell no one about him.
And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again.
He spoke of this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
But he turned and, seeing his disciples, rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For your mind is set not on the things of God but on the things of people.”
And calling the crowd to him along with his disciples, he said to them, “If anyone wants to come behind me, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.
verse.note: The Greek phrase is the same one Jesus has just used to Peter in verse 33, 'Get behind me'. Most translations render it 'come after me' here, which hides the echo: the place Peter has just been ordered back to is the disciple's proper place, behind the teacher.

Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels, and the condemned were commonly made to carry the crossbeam to the place of execution. To Mark's first readers the image was not a figure for bearing hardship but a picture of someone walking to a shameful public death.

text.q: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake and for the sake of the good news will save it.

verse.note: The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or the accession of a ruler. 'Gospel' is the traditional English equivalent and once meant just that, but it now suggests a book or a body of doctrine. Many modern translations use 'good news'; others keep 'gospel'.

text.q: For what does it profit a person to gain the whole world and forfeit their life?

verse.note: The same Greek word occurs four times in verses 35–37. It means the life or self of a living being, and it cannot mean an immaterial soul in verse 35, where it is something a person can lose for Jesus' sake. Many translations switch to 'soul' in verses 36–37; 'life' is kept throughout here so that the argument remains a single one, though the word covers more than physical survival.

text.q: For what could a person give in exchange for their life?

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of that person when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

verse.note: The charge is not chiefly sexual. Israel's prophets, notably Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, pictured the nation's unfaithfulness to God as a wife's adultery, and the word here draws on that image.

verse.text: And he said to them, “Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see that the kingdom of God has come in power.”
Six days later Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain, privately, by themselves. And he was transformed before them,
verse.note: The traditional 'transfigured' comes from the Latin translation and is now used almost only of this event. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for a change of form or appearance, and Paul uses it for the change in believers (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18). 'Transformed' gives what a first-century reader heard, though most translations keep 'transfigured'.

verse.text: and his clothes became dazzling, intensely white, whiter than any launderer on earth could whiten them.
And Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
Peter spoke up and said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
For he did not know what to say, because they were terrified.
Then a cloud came and overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is my Son, the beloved; listen to him!”
Suddenly, when they looked around, they no longer saw anyone, but only Jesus with them.
As they were coming down from the mountain, he ordered them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.
They kept the matter to themselves, debating what this rising from the dead meant.

note.traditional: they kept that saying with themselves

verse.note: The Greek can be divided two ways. Either they kept the matter to themselves, obeying the order to tell no one, or they seized on the saying and debated it among themselves. Both readings are found in modern translations.

verse.text: And they asked him, “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
verse.note: Malachi 4:5–6 promises that Elijah will be sent before the day of the Lord to restore the people, and scribal teaching drew on this. Jesus accepts the expectation and says it has already been fulfilled. Matthew's parallel (17:13) says the disciples understood him to mean John the Baptist, whose arrest and execution Mark has already told.

verse.text: He said to them, “Elijah does come first and restores all things. Yet how is it written about the Son of Man that he must suffer much and be treated with contempt?

text.q: But I tell you that Elijah has in fact come, and they did to him whatever they wanted, just as it is written about him.”

verse.text: When they came to the disciples, they saw a large crowd around them and scribes debating with them.
Immediately the whole crowd, when they saw him, were struck with amazement, and they ran up and greeted him.
He asked them, “What are you debating with them?”
One of the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you; he has a mute spirit.

text.q: Wherever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams at the mouth and grinds his teeth and goes rigid. I asked your disciples to drive it out, but they were not strong enough.”

verse.note: The verb normally means to dry up or wither. Here it may describe the boy's body stiffening during a seizure, which is how most recent translations take it. It may instead describe him becoming exhausted or wasting away over time, as older versions have it.

verse.text: He answered them, “You unbelieving generation! How long am I to be with you? How long am I to put up with you? Bring him to me.”
They brought the boy to him. When the spirit saw him, it immediately convulsed the boy, and he fell to the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth.
Jesus asked the boy’s father, “How long has this been happening to him?” He said, “Since childhood.

text.q: It has often thrown him even into fire and into water to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.”

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “‘If you can’! All things are possible for the one who believes.”
verse.note: In the earliest manuscripts Jesus throws the father's own words back at him. Many later manuscripts add 'believe', which produces the traditional 'If you can believe, all things are possible'. Editors generally regard the shorter reading as original and the addition as a scribe's attempt to smooth an abrupt phrase.

verse.text: Immediately the child’s father cried out, “I believe; help my unbelief!”
When Jesus saw that a crowd was running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you: come out of him and never enter him again.”
After crying out and convulsing him violently, it came out. The boy became like a corpse, so that most of them were saying he had died.
But Jesus took him by the hand and raised him up, and he rose to his feet.
When he had gone into a house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not drive it out?”
He said to them, “This kind can come out by nothing except prayer.”
verse.note: Most later manuscripts add 'and fasting'. The words are absent from a few of the earliest and most important manuscripts and are omitted here, following the Greek text being translated. Most scholars see them as an early addition reflecting church practice, though some defend the longer reading.

verse.text: They left that place and were passing through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know,
for he was teaching his disciples and saying to them, “The Son of Man is being handed over into human hands, and they will kill him, and when he has been killed, after three days he will rise.”
verse.note: The verb means to hand someone over into another's control. 'Betrayed' narrows it to Judas's act, but the text does not say who does the handing over; it may be Judas, or God, as in Isaiah 53 in the Greek Old Testament. The Greek also plays on 'Son of Man' being given into the hands of 'men', here rendered 'human hands'.

verse.text: But they did not understand the saying, and they were afraid to ask him.
They came to Capernaum. When he was in the house, he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?”
But they were silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest.
He sat down, called the Twelve, and said to them, “Anyone who wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.”
Then he took a little child and stood the child in their midst, and taking the child in his arms, he said to them,

text.q: “Whoever welcomes one child like this in my name welcomes me; and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.”

verse.text: John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.”
But Jesus said, “Do not stop him, for no one who does a deed of power in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me.

text.q: For whoever is not against us is for us.
For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ, truly I tell you, will certainly not lose their reward.
And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for that person if a large millstone were hung around their neck and they were thrown into the sea.

verse.note: The verb pictures tripping someone up or setting a trap in their path, and in the Gospels it is used of whatever causes a person to fall away from faith or into sin. Older versions have 'offend', which now suggests merely hurting feelings, and several modern ones have 'cause to sin'. 'Cause to stumble' keeps the image and the breadth of the Greek, and is also used by a number of modern translations.
The Greek is literally 'a donkey millstone', the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey, as distinct from the small hand mill used in a household.

text.q: And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go away into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the standard Jewish image for the place of final judgment. 'Hell' merges it with Hades and with much later imagery, so the name is kept here. Many translations still use 'hell', usually with a footnote giving Gehenna.

Verses 44 and 46 do not appear in this translation. In later manuscripts each of them repeats the words of verse 48, but they are absent from the earliest manuscripts and from the Greek text translated here. Most modern translations omit them while keeping the traditional verse numbers.

text.q: And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than, having two feet, to be thrown into Gehenna.
And if your eye causes you to stumble, throw it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God one-eyed than, having two eyes, to be thrown into Gehenna,
where ‘their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.’

note.term: their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched

verse.note: The words come from the last verse of Isaiah (66:24). There they describe the corpses of those who rebelled against God lying outside Jerusalem.

text.q: For everyone will be salted with fire.

note.traditional: For every one shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt

verse.note: Later manuscripts add 'and every sacrifice will be salted with salt', echoing Leviticus 2:13; the earliest manuscripts have only the short form translated here. The meaning of the saying is disputed. It may refer to purifying trials that every disciple undergoes, or to the fire of judgment just mentioned.

text.q: Salt is good; but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

verse.text: Setting out from there, he came into the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds again gathered around him, and as his custom was, he again taught them.
And they asked him whether a man is allowed to divorce his wife, testing him.

note.traditional: Pharisees came up and asked him

verse.note: Many manuscripts, followed by most English versions, read 'Pharisees came up and asked him'. The SBLGNT follows witnesses that lack the phrase and leave the questioners unnamed, judging the mention of Pharisees to have been added from the parallel in Matthew 19:3. Either way the questioners are hostile, as 'testing him' shows.

verse.text: He answered them, “What did Moses command you?”
They said, “Moses permitted a man to write a certificate of dismissal and to divorce her.”
But Jesus said to them, “It was because of your hardness of heart that he wrote this commandment for you.

text.q: But from the beginning of creation, ‘he made them male and female.’
‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife,
and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh.
Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

verse.text: In the house again, the disciples asked him about this.
He said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her,

text.q: and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.”

verse.note: In Jewish law as generally practised, only a husband could initiate a divorce; under Roman law a wife could do so as well. This half of the saying, found only in Mark, addresses that wider situation. Whether it reflects Jesus' own wording or an application for Mark's Gentile readers is debated.

verse.text: People were bringing children to him so that he might touch them, but the disciples rebuked them.
When Jesus saw this, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not stop them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will never enter it.”

verse.note: The Greek can mean 'as a child receives it' or 'as one receives a child'. Most interpreters take the first; the second would link the saying with 9:37, where welcoming a child is welcoming Jesus. The rendering leaves the comparison as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
As he was setting out on the road, a man ran up, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for 'age', and in Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the coming age: a matter of kind as well as length.
