Verse 30 makes the link audible, setting 'the age to come' beside 'eternal life'. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering and is kept here; a minority of translators render 'life of the age to come'.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one: God.

text.q: You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder. Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not give false testimony. Do not defraud. Honor your father and mother.’”

verse.note: This is not one of the Ten Commandments, from which the rest of the list is drawn. It may stand in for the commandment against coveting, or echo laws against withholding a worker's wages such as Deuteronomy 24:14. Why it appears here is uncertain; some suggest it is aimed at the temptations of a wealthy man.

verse.text: He said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept since my youth.”
Jesus looked at him and loved him, and said to him, “You lack one thing: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
But at this saying his face fell, and he went away grieving, for he had many possessions.
Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How hard it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!”
The disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God!

note.term: how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God!
note.traditional: how hard is it for them that trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of God

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'for those who trust in riches', and the King James tradition follows them. The earliest witnesses lack the phrase. Most scholars think it was added to soften a saying that, in its shorter form, applies to everyone.

text.q: It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: They were utterly astounded and said to one another, “Then who can be saved?”
Jesus looked at them and said, “With people it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.”
Peter began to say to him, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.”
Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for my sake and for the sake of the good news
verse.note: The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and the related verb is used in the Greek Scriptures for announcing God's saving rule. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering, but to a modern reader it suggests a book or a body of doctrine. A number of modern versions also use 'good news'.

text.q: who will not receive a hundred times as much now in this present time (houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, along with persecutions) and in the age to come, eternal life.
But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

verse.text: They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them; they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Taking the twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him:

text.q: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles,

verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one word 'Gentiles' or 'nations' according to sense. Here it refers in practice to the Roman authorities, and in verse 42 to the non-Jewish world and its rulers.

text.q: and they will mock him and spit on him and flog him and kill him, and after three days he will rise.”

verse.text: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.”
He said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Grant that we may sit, one at your right and one at your left, in your glory.”
But Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?”

note.term: be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized

verse.note: In Scripture the cup is a common image for a fate handed to someone by God, often suffering or judgment. The verb 'baptize' in ordinary Greek meant to plunge or submerge, and was used figuratively of being overwhelmed by disaster. Most interpreters take both images as pointing to Jesus' coming suffering and death, not to the rite of baptism.

verse.text: They said to him, “We can.” And Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized you will be baptized,

text.q: but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared.”

verse.text: When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant with James and John.
Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones wield authority over them.

text.q: But it is not so among you. Rather, whoever wants to become great among you will be your servant,
and whoever wants to be first among you will be slave of all.
For even the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

verse.note: The noun denotes the price paid to free a slave, a captive, or something held in pledge. The preposition translated 'for' normally means 'in place of' or 'in exchange for'. 'Many' is a Semitic way of setting the one over against the many and does not imply 'some but not all'; an echo of Isaiah 53 is widely, though not universally, recognised.

verse.text: They came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting beside the road.
When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say, “Son of David, Jesus, have mercy on me!”
Many rebuked him, telling him to be silent, but he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take courage! Get up; he is calling you.”
He threw off his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.
Jesus answered him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabbouni, let me see again.”
verse.note: Mark leaves this Aramaic word untranslated in his Greek, and it is left so here. It is a respectful form of address meaning 'my master' or 'my teacher', a heightened form of 'Rabbi'. English versions vary between 'Rabbi', 'Master', 'Lord' and 'my teacher'.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Go; your faith has saved you.” And immediately he saw again, and he followed him on the road.

note.traditional: has made you well; has healed you

verse.note: The verb covers rescue from danger, healing from illness, and salvation in the fuller sense. It is the same verb as in the disciples' question in verse 26, 'Then who can be saved?' Most versions render 'made you well' or 'healed you' here, which fits the healing but hides the link. Mark may well intend both senses, since the man at once follows Jesus on the road.

verse.text: As they approached Jerusalem, at Bethphage and Bethany near the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
and said to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied up, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it.

text.q: And if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord needs it and will send it back here immediately.’”

note.traditional: The Lord has need of it

verse.note: The Greek word means 'lord', 'master' or 'owner', so the phrase could also be heard as 'the master needs it' or even 'its owner needs it'. Most translations take it as Jesus referring to himself. The rest of the sentence is read here as part of the message, a promise to return the colt promptly; it could also be Jesus's prediction that the person will send the colt at once.

verse.text: They went off and found a colt tied at a door, outside on the street, and they untied it.
Some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?”
They answered them just as Jesus had said, and they let them go.
They brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and he sat on it.
Many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches they had cut from the fields.
Those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
verse.note: Mark leaves this Hebrew or Aramaic word untranslated in his Greek. It comes from the plea 'Save, please!' in Psalm 118:25, and the next line of the crowd's shout quotes Psalm 118:26, a psalm sung at the pilgrim festivals. By this period the word seems to have been used as a shout of acclamation as much as a prayer.

text.q: Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!”

verse.text: He entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. After looking around at everything, since the hour was already late, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.
The next day, as they were leaving Bethany, he was hungry.
Seeing from a distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see whether he might find anything on it. When he came to it he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

note.term: for it was not the season for figs
note.traditional: for it was not the season for figs

verse.note: Around Passover a fig tree in leaf would not yet have ripe figs, as Mark himself points out. Most interpreters therefore read the episode as an acted sign rather than an outburst of frustration. Mark wraps the fig tree story around the action in the temple, so that each interprets the other.

verse.text: He said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again!” And his disciples were listening.

They came to Jerusalem. Entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling and those who were buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves,
verse.note: The Greek word here refers to the whole temple complex with its courts, not the sanctuary building itself. The trading took place in the large outer court. Money changers exchanged pilgrims' currency for the coinage accepted for temple dues, and doves were the sacrifice offered by those who could not afford a larger animal.

verse.text: and he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
He was teaching and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of bandits.”
verse.note: The quotation is from Isaiah 56:7. The Greek word translated 'nations' here is the same word rendered 'Gentiles' elsewhere in this translation; in the plural it means the non-Jewish peoples. The outer court was the one part of the temple that non-Jews could enter.

The phrase comes from Jeremiah 7:11. The Greek word means a violent brigand or outlaw, not a cheat or petty thief; it is the same word used later for the men crucified with Jesus. In Jeremiah the image is of a hideout where bandits retreat to feel safe after their crimes, so the charge is probably not only about dishonest trading. Most translations keep 'robbers'.

verse.text: The chief priests and the scribes heard this and began looking for a way to destroy him; for they were afraid of him, because the whole crowd was astounded at his teaching.
When evening came, they went out of the city.
verse.note: The Greek construction can describe a single occasion or a repeated one: 'whenever evening came, they would go out of the city', meaning each night of that week. Translations are divided. Some manuscripts also read 'he went out' rather than 'they went out'.

verse.text: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots.
Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree you cursed has withered.”
Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in their heart but believes that what they say is happening, it will be so for them.
For this reason I tell you, everything you pray and ask for, believe that you have received it, and it will be so for you.
And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive you your offenses.”

verse.note: The Greek is plural here, a Semitic turn of phrase reflecting Hebrew and Aramaic usage, and this translation keeps it. Most English versions flatten it to 'heaven'. Where the Greek is singular, as in verses 30 and 31, 'heaven' is used.

The traditional 'trespasses' now suggests entering someone's property without permission. The Greek word means a false step or wrong done against someone, which fits the context of having something against another person. Some modern versions use 'sins', but that is the usual rendering of a different Greek word.

note.term: may also forgive you your offenses

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add a verse 26: 'But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your trespasses.' It is absent from the earliest manuscripts and was probably added under the influence of Matthew 6:15. The edition translated here omits it, which is why the numbering passes from 25 to 27.

verse.text: They came again to Jerusalem. As he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came to him
and said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things? Or who gave you this authority to do these things?”
Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question. Answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things.

text.q: The baptism of John—was it from heaven or from human beings? Answer me.”

verse.note: 'Heaven' here is a reverent Jewish way of saying 'God' without naming him. The question is whether John's baptism was authorised by God or was merely a human undertaking.

verse.text: They discussed it among themselves, saying, “What should we say? If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’
verse.note: These words are missing from many manuscripts and from several critical editions and translations, which begin the deliberation with 'If we say'. The edition translated here includes them. The sense of the passage is not affected.

verse.text: But should we say, ‘From human beings’?” They were afraid of the crowd, for everyone held that John really was a prophet.
So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Then neither am I telling you by what authority I do these things.”
And he began to speak to them in parables: “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a vat for the winepress, and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went abroad.
verse.note: The fence, the winepress vat and the tower echo the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5:1–7, where the vineyard is Israel and its owner is God. Hearers who knew that passage would have recognised the picture at once and taken the tenants to be those entrusted with Israel. Absentee owners leasing land to tenants for a share of the crop was a familiar arrangement.

text.q: At the season he sent a slave to the tenants, to collect from the tenants a share of the vineyard’s fruit.

verse.note: The Greek word means a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most older English versions soften it to 'servant'; several recent ones use 'slave'. In the Septuagint the prophets are called God's slaves, which is probably part of the parable's point.

text.q: But they seized him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.
Again he sent them another slave; that one they struck on the head and treated shamefully.

verse.note: This form of the verb is found nowhere else in surviving Greek, so its meaning has to be inferred from its evident connection with the word for 'head' and from the context. 'Struck on the head' is the usual understanding, but the precise sense is uncertain. Later manuscripts add that the tenants stoned him.

text.q: He sent another, and that one they killed; and so with many others, beating some and killing others.
He still had one, a beloved son. He sent him to them last of all, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’
So they seized him and killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.
What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants, and give the vineyard to others.
Have you not even read this scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone;

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 118:22–23 in its Greek form. The phrase is literally 'head of the corner' and may mean either a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the stone that crowns it, such as a capstone. Scholars are divided; either way it is the most important stone, and the builders had rejected it.

text.q: this came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”

verse.text: They were looking for a way to arrest him, but they feared the crowd, for they knew that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
Then they sent to him some of the Pharisees and of the Herodians, to trap him in what he said.

They came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and defer to no one, for you show no partiality but truly teach the way of God. Is it permitted to give the poll tax to Caesar or not? Should we give it or should we not?”
verse.note: The word is borrowed from Latin census and refers to the head tax Rome levied on Judea after it came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, payable in Roman coin. Its introduction had provoked an armed revolt, and it remained a symbol of subjection. A plain yes would discredit Jesus with the crowd; a plain no could be reported as sedition.

verse.text: But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said to them, “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius so that I can look at it.”
They brought one. And he said to them, “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.”
Jesus said to them, “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” And they were utterly amazed at him.
verse.note: The questioners asked whether to 'give' the tax; Jesus answers with a compound verb that means to give back or pay what is owed. 'Render' once said this but is now obscure. The coin bears Caesar's image and so is treated as his; many interpreters hear an unstated counterpart, that people bear God's image, but the text does not say so.

verse.text: Then Sadducees came to him, who say there is no resurrection, and they put a question to him:

text.q: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves behind a wife but leaves no child, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.
There were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and when he died he left no offspring.
The second took her, and died leaving no offspring behind; and the third likewise.
None of the seven left offspring. Last of all the woman died too.
In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.”

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Is this not why you are mistaken: that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?

text.q: For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in the heavens.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God's dwelling that this translation keeps where it occurs. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'.

text.q: And as for the dead, that they are raised: have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?

note.term: in the passage about the bush

verse.note: The Greek says only 'at the bush'. Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage was cited by its subject; this is the burning bush account in Exodus 3. The Sadducees are answered from the books of Moses, which they themselves had quoted as their authority.

text.q: He is not God of the dead but of the living. You are badly mistaken.”

verse.text: One of the scribes came up and heard them debating. Seeing that Jesus had answered them well, he asked him, “Which commandment is first of all?”
Jesus answered, “The first is: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one,

note.term: the Lord our God, the Lord is one
note.traditional: The Lord our God is one Lord

verse.note: This is Deuteronomy 6:4, the opening of the Shema, the confession devout Jews recited daily. The Greek, like the Hebrew behind it, can also be read 'the Lord our God is one Lord' or 'the Lord is our God, the Lord alone'. The rendering here follows the scribe's own summary in verse 32, 'he is one'.

text.q: and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’
The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

verse.text: The scribe said to him, “Well said, Teacher. You have spoken truly: he is one, and there is no other besides him;

text.q: and to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is far more than all the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”

verse.text: Jesus, seeing that he had answered thoughtfully, said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to question him any more.
While teaching in the temple, Jesus spoke up and said, “How can the scribes say that the Messiah is David’s son?
verse.note: The Greek word means 'anointed one' and here is a title for the king Israel expected, not a name for Jesus. 'Messiah' conveys the title to a modern reader, while 'Christ' is kept where the word functions as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: David himself said, in the Holy Spirit, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet.”’

note.term: The Lord said to my Lord

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew the first 'Lord' is the divine name and the second is an ordinary word for a superior, 'my lord'; the Greek version uses the same word for both. The argument assumes that David is the speaker and that the one he addresses is the Messiah, so that David calls his own descendant his superior.

verse.text: David himself calls him Lord; so how can he be his son?” And the large crowd was listening to him gladly.
And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and to be greeted in the marketplaces,

text.q: and to have the front seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.
They devour widows’ houses and for show make long prayers. These will receive a harsher judgment.”

verse.text: Sitting down opposite the treasury, he watched how the crowd was putting money into the treasury. Many rich people were putting in large amounts.
Then one poor widow came and put in two tiny coins, together worth a quadrans.

note.term: two tiny coins, together worth a quadrans
note.traditional: two mites, which make a farthing

verse.note: The lepton was the smallest coin in circulation in Judea. Mark explains its value in Roman terms for his readers: two made one quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, a sixty-fourth of a denarius, and a denarius was roughly a day's wage for a laborer. Renderings such as 'penny' or 'farthing' give the general idea but no real sense of the amount.

verse.text: Calling his disciples to him, he said to them, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are putting into the treasury.

text.q: For they all put in out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”

verse.text: As he was going out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Teacher, look! What stones, and what buildings!”
And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”
As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John and Andrew asked him privately,

text.q: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?”

verse.text: Jesus began to say to them, “Watch out that no one leads you astray.

text.q: Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will lead many astray.

verse.note: The Greek is simply “I am.” Most take it as a claim to be the Messiah, which is how Matthew's parallel spells it out. Some hear an echo of the divine self-designation of the Greek Old Testament, so that the impostors claim more than a title.

text.q: When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. It must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom; there will be earthquakes in place after place; there will be famines. These things are the beginning of the birth pains.

verse.note: The same Greek word lies behind “nation” here, “nations” in verse 10, and “Gentiles” elsewhere in this translation. In verse 10 “all the nations” could also be heard as “all the Gentiles”; the wider sense is chosen because the scope is the whole world.

text.q: But you, watch out for yourselves. They will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them.

note.traditional: for a testimony against them / as a witness to them

verse.note: The Greek dative can mean testimony given to the rulers or testimony that will count against them. Translations divide. The link with verse 10, where the good news is proclaimed to all nations, favours “to them,” but the hostile sense is possible.

text.q: And the good news must first be proclaimed to all the nations.
And when they lead you away to hand you over, do not worry beforehand about what you will say, but say whatever is given to you in that hour, for it is not you who are speaking but the Holy Spirit.
Brother will hand brother over to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and have them put to death.
And you will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

verse.text: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he must not be” (let the reader understand) “then those in Judea must flee to the mountains;
verse.note: The phrase comes from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it refers to a sacrilege that defiles the temple and leaves it desolate. Jewish readers connected it with the pagan altar that Antiochus IV set up in the Jerusalem temple in 167 BC. Jesus uses it for a comparable outrage still to come; what event is meant is debated.

note.term: standing where he must not be

verse.note: The Greek noun for “abomination” is neuter, but the participle “standing” is masculine, which suggests that Mark has a person in view. Many translations nevertheless use “it.” The grammatical mismatch is deliberate enough that “he” is kept here.

Most scholars take this as Mark's own aside to whoever reads his book aloud, signalling that the cryptic phrase needs decoding. It is treated here as the narrator's words. The alternative is that Jesus himself is speaking, referring to the reader of Daniel.

text.q: the one on the housetop must not come down or go in to take anything out of his house,
and the one in the field must not turn back to get his cloak.
Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days!
Pray that it may not happen in winter.
For those days will be a distress such as has never been, from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be.

verse.note: The Greek word is an ordinary term for severe pressure, hardship or suffering. “Tribulation” has become a technical term in some end-times schemes, which it was not for the first readers. The wording echoes Daniel 12:1.

text.q: And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no flesh would have been saved. But for the sake of the chosen, whom he chose, he has cut short the days.

verse.note: The traditional “the elect” hides the fact that the noun and the verb are the same word in Greek and now sounds like a doctrinal term. In the Septuagint the word describes Israel as the people God chose. “The chosen” is used again in verses 22 and 27.

text.q: And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Look, there he is!’ do not believe it.

verse.note: The Greek word is traditionally rendered “Christ.” Here it is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, rather than a name for Jesus, so “Messiah” is used; “false messiahs” in verse 22 follows suit. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels.

text.q: For false messiahs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the chosen.
But you, watch out. I have told you everything beforehand.
But in those days, after that distress, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light,
and the stars will be falling from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.

note.term: the Son of Man coming in clouds

verse.note: The language is drawn from Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion. The darkened sun and moon and the falling stars in verses 24–25 likewise echo the prophets (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4), who used such imagery for God's judgment on nations.

text.q: And then he will send out the angels and gather the chosen from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of the sky.
Learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near.
So also you, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, at the doors.

note.traditional: it is near / he is near

verse.note: The Greek verb has no expressed subject, so “it is near” (the end, or the event just described) is equally possible. “He” is chosen because the Son of Man has just been mentioned and because the image of someone at the doors is picked up in the returning master of verses 34–36.

text.q: Truly I tell you, this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things have taken place.

verse.note: The most natural sense is Jesus's own contemporaries, and that is how the phrase is used elsewhere in Mark. Because this is hard to reconcile with the coming of the Son of Man, others have proposed the Jewish people, humanity, or the generation that sees the signs. It is also disputed whether “all these things” covers the whole discourse or only the events leading to the temple's destruction in AD 70.

text.q: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
But about that day or hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
Watch out, stay alert, for you do not know when the time is.

verse.note: Most manuscripts add “and pray” after “stay alert.” A few early witnesses lack the words, and the Greek text followed here omits them as a probable addition influenced by 14:38.

text.q: It is like a man away on a journey: he left his house and gave authority to his slaves, to each his work, and he commanded the doorkeeper to stay awake.

verse.note: The Greek word means a slave, someone owned by a master, not a hired servant. Many English versions soften it to “servants.” The household Jesus describes is one in which the owner's slaves run his affairs in his absence.

text.q: So stay awake, for you do not know when the master of the house is coming, whether in the evening or at midnight or at cockcrow or at dawn,

note.term: whether in the evening or at midnight or at cockcrow or at dawn

verse.note: These are the popular names of the four watches into which the Roman system divided the night, each about three hours long. The master may return during any of them.

text.q: so that he does not come suddenly and find you sleeping.
And what I say to you I say to everyone: stay awake.”

verse.text: It was now two days before the Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to seize him by stealth and kill him,
for they said, “Not during the festival, or there may be a riot among the people.”
While he was in Bethany, reclining at table in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came with an alabaster flask of very costly perfume, pure nard. She broke the flask and poured it over his head.
verse.note: The adjective describing the nard is rare and its meaning is uncertain. Most scholars connect it with the word for “trustworthy” and take it to mean genuine or unadulterated, which is the reading followed here. Others have proposed “liquid” or a trade name for a particular variety of nard.

verse.text: But some were saying indignantly to one another, “Why this waste of the perfume?
This perfume could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.” And they scolded her harshly.

note.traditional: three hundred denarii; three hundred pence

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a labourer. Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year’s wages, which explains the indignation of the onlookers.

verse.text: But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why are you making trouble for her? She has done a good deed for me.

text.q: For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want you can do good to them; but you do not always have me.
She did what she could: she has anointed my body beforehand for its burial.
Truly I tell you, wherever the good news is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

verse.note: The Greek word meant good news or its announcement, such as news of a victory or a ruler’s accession, and the Greek Old Testament uses the related verb for announcing God’s reign. “Gospel” originally meant the same in English but now suggests a book or a religious category. Many modern translations use “good news” in at least some places.

verse.text: Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went off to the chief priests to hand him over to them.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for handing someone or something over. Mark uses it for John’s arrest, for the Son of Man being handed over to human hands, and for the priests handing Jesus to Pilate. Most translations use “betray” when Judas is the subject, which fits the act but hides that the same word runs through the whole passion story. Greek has a separate word for treachery, which Mark does not use.

verse.text: When they heard this they were glad, and they promised to give him money. So he began looking for a good opportunity to hand him over.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, his disciples said to him, “Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
He sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,

text.q: and wherever he goes in, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says: Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’
He will show you a large upstairs room, furnished and ready. Prepare for us there.”

verse.text: The disciples set out and went into the city and found everything just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.
As they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over, one who is eating with me.”
They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, “Surely not I?”
He said to them, “One of the Twelve, the one dipping into the bowl with me.

text.q: For the Son of Man goes just as it is written about him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”

verse.text: While they were eating, he took bread, said a blessing, broke it and gave it to them, and said, “Take it; this is my body.”
Then he took a cup, gave thanks and gave it to them, and they all drank from it.
He said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

text.q: Truly I tell you, I will never again drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’

text.q: But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

verse.text: Peter said to him, “Even if they all fall away, I will not.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today, this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”
But he kept insisting all the more, “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you.” And they all said the same.
They came to a place named Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He took Peter, James and John with him, and he began to be overcome with dread and anguish,
and he said to them, “My soul is deeply sorrowful, to the point of death. Remain here and stay awake.”
Going a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass him by.
He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Take this cup away from me. Yet not what I want, but what you want.”
verse.note: Abba is the Aramaic word for “father”, and Mark gives the Greek translation beside it. It was used by adult children as well as small ones, so the popular claim that it means “Daddy” goes beyond the evidence. It is nonetheless a direct and familiar form of address to God.

verse.text: He came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Did you not have the strength to stay awake one hour?

text.q: Stay awake and pray, so that you do not come into testing. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

verse.note: The Greek word covers both a trial that tests a person and an enticement to do wrong. English “temptation” now suggests only the second. With the arrest moments away, the sense here is the ordeal that will test the disciples’ loyalty. Most translations keep “temptation”; some have “the time of trial”.

verse.text: Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.
And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
He came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.
verse.note: This single Greek word is one of the most obscure in Mark. “It is enough” is the traditional guess; other proposals include “it is settled” and “the account is paid”, the latter from the verb’s use on commercial receipts. The words before it can also be read as a command (“Sleep on now and rest”) and not as a question. No solution has general agreement.

text.q: Get up, let us go. Look, the one handing me over has come near.”

verse.text: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, the scribes and the elders.
Now the one handing him over had given them a signal, saying, “The one I kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away securely.”
When he arrived, he went up to him at once and said, “Rabbi!” and he kissed him.
They laid hands on him and seized him.
But one of those standing by drew his sword and struck the high priest’s slave, cutting off his ear.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Many English versions soften it to “servant”; several recent ones use “slave”, as here.

verse.text: Jesus responded to them, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if against a bandit?
verse.note: The word denotes someone who plunders with violence, a brigand or outlaw, not a burglar or pickpocket. Writers of the period also applied it to armed insurgents, and some translations render it “rebel” or “revolutionary” here. Mark uses the same word for the two men crucified with Jesus.

text.q: Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But this is so that the scriptures may be fulfilled.”

verse.text: Then they all left him and fled.
A certain young man was following along with him, wearing nothing but a linen cloth over his bare body. They seized him,
but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.
They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders and the scribes assembled.
Peter followed him from a distance, right inside the courtyard of the high priest, and he was sitting with the attendants and warming himself at the fire.
The chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus so as to put him to death, but they could find none.
For many were giving false testimony against him, but their testimonies did not agree.
Then some stood up and gave false testimony against him, saying,

text.q: “We heard him say, ‘I will tear down this sanctuary made by hands, and in three days I will build another not made by hands.’”

verse.note: Mark uses two Greek words that English versions usually both translate “temple”. One refers to the whole temple complex with its courts (as in verse 49), and the one used here refers to the sanctuary building itself. The translation keeps them distinct, though scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers observe the difference.

verse.text: Yet not even on this did their testimony agree.
Then the high priest stood up in the middle and questioned Jesus, saying, “Do you make no answer at all? What is it these men are testifying against you?”
But he kept silent and answered nothing. Again the high priest questioned him and said to him, “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?”
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew title Messiah, the anointed king Israel expected. Here the high priest is asking about that title, not using a name, so “Messiah” is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction, keeping “Christ” where it works as a name.

verse.text: Jesus said, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”
verse.note: “The Power”, like “the Blessed One” in the high priest’s question, is a reverent way of referring to God without naming him. Jesus’ answer combines the language of Psalm 110:1 (seated at God’s right hand) and Daniel 7:13 (one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven).

verse.text: The high priest tore his clothes and said, “Why do we still need witnesses?
You have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” And they all condemned him as deserving death.
Then some began to spit on him, to cover his face, to strike him with their fists and to say to him, “Prophesy!” And the attendants took him and slapped him.
While Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s slave girls came by,
and when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked straight at him and said, “You too were with the Nazarene, Jesus.”
But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you are talking about.” And he went outside into the forecourt, and a rooster crowed.
verse.note: These words are absent from several of the earliest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and some critical editions bracket them. SBLGNT prints them. They prepare for the “second time” in verse 72, which may be why a copyist added them or the reason they are original.

verse.text: The slave girl saw him and began again to say to those standing by, “This man is one of them.”
But he denied it again. A little later those standing by again said to Peter, “You really are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech is like theirs.”

note.term: and your speech is like theirs

verse.note: These words are printed in SBLGNT but are missing from the earliest manuscripts and from most other modern critical editions, and so from many English translations. Many scholars think they were added by copyists under the influence of Matthew 26:73.

verse.text: But he began to call down curses and to swear, “I do not know this man you are talking about.”
verse.note: The verb means to invoke a solemn curse, not to use foul language. The Greek gives no object. Most translations understand Peter to be calling a curse on himself if he is lying; some scholars argue that he is cursing Jesus. The translation leaves the object unstated, as Mark does.

verse.text: And immediately a rooster crowed a second time. Then Peter remembered what Jesus had said to him: “Before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.

note.traditional: when he thought on it, he wept; he broke down and wept

verse.note: The Greek participle here literally means “having thrown upon”, and its sense in this sentence is uncertain. Proposals include “he broke down”, “when he thought about it”, “he began to” and “covering his head”. The rendering follows the most common modern choice.

verse.text: As soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. They bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.
Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” He answered him, “You say so.”

note.traditional: Thou sayest it / You have said so

verse.note: The Greek is two words, literally “You say.” It can be read as a qualified yes (“It is as you say”), as a non-committal reply that throws the claim back on the questioner (“Those are your words”), or even as a question. Most scholars take it as deliberately reserved; Pilate’s continued questioning suggests he did not hear a plain confession.

verse.text: And the chief priests kept accusing him of many things.
Pilate questioned him again: “Have you no answer at all? See how many things they accuse you of.”
But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
Now at the festival he used to release for them one prisoner, whichever one they asked for.
The man called Barabbas was in prison with the insurgents who had committed murder in the insurrection.
The crowd came up and began to ask him to do what he usually did for them.
Pilate answered them, “Do you want me to release for you the king of the Jews?”
For he realized that the chief priests had handed him over out of envy.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas for them instead.
Pilate spoke to them again: “Then what do you want me to do with the man you call the king of the Jews?”
They shouted back, “Crucify him!”
Pilate said to them, “Why? What wrong has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him!”
So Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them. He had Jesus flogged and handed him over to be crucified.
The soldiers led him away inside the palace, that is, the governor’s headquarters, and called together the whole cohort.
verse.note: Mark uses the Latin word praetorium, the official residence of a Roman governor. In Jerusalem this was probably either Herod’s former palace or the Antonia fortress beside the temple; which one is disputed. A cohort was nominally several hundred soldiers, though “the whole cohort” may simply mean all who were on duty.

verse.text: They dressed him in purple, and after weaving a crown of thorns they put it on him.
Then they began to salute him: “Hail, king of the Jews!”
They kept striking him on the head with a reed and spitting on him, and falling on their knees they bowed down before him.
When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple and dressed him in his own clothes. Then they led him out to crucify him.
They pressed into service a passer-by who was coming in from the country, a certain Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.

note.term: the father of Alexander and Rufus

verse.note: The two sons play no part in the story, and only Mark names them. The natural explanation is that they were known to Mark’s first readers. A Rufus is greeted in Romans 16:13, but whether he is the same person is uncertain.

verse.text: They brought him to the place Golgotha, which translated means Place of a Skull.
They tried to give him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it.
And they crucified him and divided his clothes among themselves, casting lots for them to decide who should take what.
It was the third hour when they crucified him.
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning, the sixth (v. 33) about noon, and the ninth (vv. 33–34) about three in the afternoon. John 19:14 gives a different time for the proceedings, a difficulty for which several explanations have been offered and none is agreed.

verse.text: The inscription stating the charge against him read: “The King of the Jews.”
With him they crucified two bandits, one on his right and one on his left.
verse.note: The Greek word means someone who takes by violence, a brigand or armed raider, not a sneak thief, for which Greek has a different word. Josephus uses it of insurgent bands in Judea, and some translations therefore render it “rebels” here; that sense is possible, especially after v. 7, but is not certain. “Bandits” keeps the element of violence without deciding the question.

note.term: one on his right and one on his left

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add a verse 28: “And the scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was counted among the lawless.’” It is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably borrowed from Luke 22:37. The edition translated here omits it, which is why the numbering passes from 27 to 29.

verse.text: Those who passed by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads and saying, “Ha! You who would destroy the temple and build it in three days,

text.q: save yourself by coming down from the cross!”

verse.text: In the same way the chief priests too, along with the scribes, mocked him among themselves, saying, “He saved others; himself he cannot save!
Let the Messiah, the king of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe.” Even those who were crucified with him taunted him.
verse.note: The Greek christos means “anointed one” and here is a title, set alongside “the king of Israel” in the priests’ taunt. “Messiah” conveys the title, whereas “Christ” now sounds to most readers like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice, using “Messiah” in the Gospels where the title is the point and “Christ” elsewhere.

verse.text: When the sixth hour came, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean a particular land or region, or the earth as a whole. Mark may mean darkness over Judea or over the whole world; the text does not decide. Some translations have “the whole earth.”

verse.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which translated means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
verse.note: These are the opening words of Psalm 22 in Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus and his followers, which Mark writes out in Greek letters and then translates. The same psalm lies behind earlier details of the scene: the dividing of clothes by lot (v. 24) and the mockers shaking their heads (v. 29). In v. 35 the bystanders take the words as a call to Elijah, who was expected to come to the aid of the righteous in distress.

verse.text: Some of those standing by heard it and said, “Look, he is calling Elijah!”
Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait! Let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”
But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed his last.
And the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.
verse.note: The temple had two great curtains: one at the entrance to the sanctuary building and one inside it, screening off the Most Holy Place. Mark does not say which is meant; most interpreters think the inner one, but this is disputed. The verb “torn” is the one Mark used of the heavens at Jesus’s baptism (1:10).

verse.text: When the centurion who stood facing him saw that he breathed his last in this way, he said, “Truly this man was God’s Son!”
verse.note: The Greek has no article and can be translated “the Son of God” or “a son of God.” On the lips of a Roman soldier the phrase could mean something like a divine or godlike man, and some translations render it that way. Mark, however, plainly means his readers to hear the confession that opens his book (1:1). “God’s Son” leaves both possibilities open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: There were also women watching from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome,
who used to follow him and serve him when he was in Galilee, and many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem.
When evening had already come, since it was Preparation day, that is, the day before the Sabbath,
Joseph of Arimathea came, a respected council member who was himself also waiting for the kingdom of God. He took courage, went in to Pilate, and asked for the body of Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a member of a city council. It is usually understood here to mean a member of the Jerusalem council that condemned Jesus, though Mark uses a different word for that body in v. 1 and does not say so explicitly. The adjective translated “respected” can also imply wealth and social standing.

verse.text: Pilate was amazed that he was already dead, and summoning the centurion he asked him whether he had been dead for long.
When he learned from the centurion that it was so, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the cloth, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where he was laid.
When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they could go and anoint him.
And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen.

note.term: the first day of the week
note.traditional: the first day of the week

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'the one of the sabbaths'. In Jewish Greek the word for Sabbath, especially in the plural, also meant the seven-day week, so the phrase means the day after the Sabbath, that is, Sunday.

verse.text: They were saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?”
And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was extremely large.
Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verse.note: Mark calls the figure simply a young man. The white robe and the message he delivers mark him as a heavenly messenger, and Matthew's parallel account speaks of an angel. Most interpreters read Mark the same way, though Mark himself does not use the word.

verse.text: But he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look, the place where they laid him.
verse.note: The Greek verb is passive in form. It can be read as a true passive, 'he has been raised' (that is, by God), or as an intransitive, 'he has risen'. Both are grammatically possible; the passive is chosen here because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus, but the traditional rendering is not wrong.

text.q: But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’”

verse.note: This points back to Jesus' words on the way to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:28), where he told the disciples that after being raised he would go ahead of them into Galilee.

verse.text: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and bewilderment had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. ⟦But everything they had been instructed they reported briefly to Peter and those with him. And after this Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation. Amen.⟧
verse.note: The two earliest complete manuscripts of Mark, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (fourth century), end the Gospel with these words, and most scholars hold this to be the earliest ending that can be recovered. Whether Mark meant to stop this abruptly or an original ending was lost is disputed.

note.term: But everything they had been instructed

verse.note: The double brackets mark the so-called shorter ending, which the Greek edition translated here prints as a later addition rather than part of Mark's own text. It is found in only a small number of manuscripts, almost always followed by the longer ending (verses 9–20), and its vocabulary is unlike Mark's.

verse.text: ⟦Now having risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven out seven demons.

note.term: Now having risen early on the first day of the week

verse.note: The double brackets around verses 9–20 mark the longer ending. It appears in the great majority of manuscripts and was known by the late second century, but it is absent from the two earliest, joins awkwardly to verse 8, and differs from Mark in style and vocabulary. Nearly all scholars regard it as an early addition that draws on the resurrection accounts in the other Gospels and Acts; many churches nonetheless receive it as Scripture.

verse.text: She went and told those who had been with him, who were mourning and weeping.
And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe it.
After this he showed himself in a different form to two of them as they were walking, on their way into the country.
They too went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them either.

Later he showed himself to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had been raised.
And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary one for good news, especially a public announcement of a victory or a ruler's accession. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and originally meant the same thing, but for many modern readers it has become a purely religious term or the name of a kind of book.

The Greek noun can mean creation as a whole or an individual created being, so the phrase can also be read 'to every creature', as in older English versions. In either case the sense is all humanity without restriction.

text.q: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new languages;

verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for the tongue and, by extension, a language. 'Tongues' is the traditional rendering and once meant simply 'languages', but in modern English it suggests a special religious phenomenon rather than what a Greek reader would have heard. How the speech described here relates to that in Acts 2 and 1 Corinthians 12–14 is debated.

text.q: they will pick up snakes, and if they drink anything deadly it will certainly not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will get well.”

verse.text: So then the Lord Jesus, after speaking to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.

note.term: sat down at the right hand of God

verse.note: The wording echoes Psalm 110:1 ('Sit at my right hand'), the passage early Christians most often used to describe Jesus' exaltation. The seat at a king's right hand was the place of highest honour and shared authority.

verse.text: And they went out and proclaimed everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message through the signs that followed.⟧
